notes: Concerns which of landlord/lessee bears health-department penalty liability for a leased tenement house; no bearing on compensated room-letting or lodging.

holding_summary: In recounting the facts underlying a widow's claim against her husband's estate, the court recites, without any adverse comment, that she had run a boarding-house before and throughout her marriage in her own house, and for a period rented furnished rooms instead, as her ordinary business.

quotes.text: Subsequent to the marriage, the claimant continued to keep boarders, in a house owned and furnished by her, for nearly the entire seventeen years of her married life, and the business was only interrupted for a few years during which she rented part of her house in furnished rooms.

notes: Court does not doctrinally classify the arrangement (lease/license/lodging/innkeeping); the boarding-house facts are background to a probate claim resolved on consideration/gratuitous-support grounds, so characterization is left null.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: Under chapter 446 of the Laws of 1899, a boarding-house keeper has a lien on a boarder's property for the amount due for board, practically equivalent to an innkeeper's common-law lien, and tender of the amount due extinguishes it.

quotes.text: by chapter 446, Laws of 1899, a boarding-house keeper is given a lien “ for the amount which may be due for board.” His lien is practically the same as that of an innkeeper.

holding_summary: An occupant who resides in hotel rooms for an extended period under an open-ended arrangement (here roughly sixteen months) ceases to be a 'guest' subject to the innkeeper's strict common-law liability for lost property; even if the innkeeper-guest relation existed at first, it is lost through lapse of time as the occupancy becomes that of a permanent lodger.

quotes.text: the Annex was the plaintiff’s home; her permanent abiding place; and that she wtas not there merely for temporary accommodation or as a transient guest.
if such was the case that relationship, by the lapse of time, was lost long before her property was lost.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: Absent an express covenant restricting an 'Apartment Hotel' exclusively to leased apartments, the landlord may also lease other rooms in the building to transient guests by the day; doing so does not breach the term tenant's lease or constitute a constructive eviction.

quotes.text: The plaintiff leased to the defendant a suite of rooms in the building described in the lease as the “ Bristol Apartment Hotel”, and defendant entered into the occupancy of the rooms and paid rent for eight months.

it by no means follows, in the absence of an express covenant that no portion of the building would be rented otherwise than in apartments as aforesaid, that plaintiff was guilty of a breach of any contract with defendant when it undertook to lease rooms in the building to transient tenants.

court: County Court of New York, Orleans County
notes: Farmhand's occupancy of employer's house was an incident of a farm-labor hiring contract (license vs. tenancy for wrongful-discharge purposes), not compensated lodging/boarding let by a householder.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: Although letting an apartment in a hotel ordinarily creates a landlord-tenant relationship, a contract to furnish an apartment together with board for a family at a single weekly price is not an ordinary lease, because furnishing the board is the most substantial part of the consideration; damages for breach are limited to the price less the landlord's saved cost of the board.

quotes.text: it is equally true that the contract in question here is not analogous to an ordinary lease of premises.
an agreement for the letting of an apartment in an apartment hotel ordinarily creates the relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties
The furnishing of the board, therefore, was not merely incidental to the renting of the premises, but was, in fact, a very substantial, if not the most substantial, part of the contract.

notes: Concerns municipal regulation of taxicab hack stands under the police power; hotels appear only as abutting property owners, with no bearing on room-letting or lodging.

holding_summary: Property used to house and board outside paying guests, even when operated by a religious missionary organization, is not used exclusively for exempt purposes and loses its tax exemption as to the parcels so used, though a separate parcel used only to house missionary families and staff remains exempt.

quotes.text: It had hired out on some occasions the advantages of these parcels to persons in no way connected with its missionary undertakings and had received an income which it applied to expenses. This user, however, took from it the right of exemption.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: Where a tenant occupies part of a leased dwelling and sublets other rooms to roomers under weekly hirings for more than a week, the sublet portions are used for business, not dwelling, purposes, and are therefore outside the protection of the rent laws applicable to dwellings.

quotes.text: where three floors out of five are leased to roomers upon a weekly tenancy for more than a week, such parts of the premises so leased are used for business and not for dwelling purposes.
